items.title: Brent spikes to $105.50 on Houthi/Saudi attacks, fades to $103.40 — market stops paying full geopolitical premium
items.idea: Brent printed above $105.50 after fresh Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and renewed tanker trouble near Hormuz, then slid to ~$103.40 on Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim for Russia/Ukraine. The author's read: the retreat matters more than the spike — futures no longer treat every escalation as the start of a straight-line inflation shock, while physical tightness keeps Brent above $100.
items.angle: Fading headline premia while physical stays tight is the exact setup where gap risk lives. Pair with HFIR's record Brent short positioning.
items.tweetA: Houthis hit Saudi infrastructure and Brent gives it all back in hours. Either the market has learned to discount headlines, or it is short gamma into a physical squeeze. Positioning data says the second. $USO $BNO
items.tweetB: A Russia-Ukraine 'energy ceasefire' headline was enough to erase a Saudi-attack spike. That is a market pricing diplomacy at full value and sabotage at zero. I would not want to be the one holding that asymmetry. $XLE

items.title: 10-year brushed 5.4% — highest since 2002 — and the S&P still hit a record
items.idea: The 10-year approached 5.4% last week, the highest since 2002. The S&P 500 set a record Tuesday, stumbled on AI-demand worries, then recovered Friday on earnings. The author says 5% can be rationalised as nominal growth, but materially beyond that becomes 'a tax on duration, financing and valuations'; the bulls win only while earnings outrun the cost of capital.
items.angle: Equity-bond correlation regime: stocks are carrying a 2002 discount rate on 2026 multiples. Narrow winners doing the lifting.
items.tweetA: 10y at 5.4% = highest since 2002. S&P at a record. In 2002 the S&P traded on about 15x and the market was cleaning up an equity bust. What exactly is being priced now that makes both true? $SPY $TLT
items.tweetB: Equities are underwriting 5.4% with earnings revisions alone. That works until the revision breadth narrows, and the author says it is already leaning on the same few winners. Watch equal-weight vs cap-weight into CPI.

items.title: CPI week: bond market already tightening for the Fed — how much hiking is left to do if long yields do the work?
items.idea: With Fed Chair Kevin Warsh scheduled to speak, the framing shifts from 'will the Fed hike again' to 'how much official tightening is needed when market rates already tighten'. Soft CPI keeps the Fed patient while the long end works; hot CPI reopens a hike and pushes the long end back to highs.
items.angle: Reaction-function trade: a hot print hits both ends, a soft print can still keep term premium bid via oil. Curve steepener vs level.
items.tweetA: If the long end is doing the Fed's job, a hot CPI forces a choice: hike into 5.4% or let term premium run. Neither is a good outcome for duration. The only good print is a boring one. $TLT $ZN
items.tweetB: Warsh inherits a market that already hiked for him. Every extra 25bp from the Fed now lands on a curve that is pricing fiscal and oil risk on its own. Hard to tell where the Fed's tightening ends and the market's begins.

items.title: Gold up three straight days, back above $4,200, while equities hold: owning risk but not discarding protection
items.idea: Gold has risen three days in a row to above $4,200 even as US futures are firmer, the dollar stays firm and Korea softens. The author's tell: investors 'are still willing to own risk but not willing to throw away protection' — one hand on the throttle, one on the brake.
items.angle: Gold and a firm dollar and 5.4% yields at once is unusual; monetary-hedge demand is running through real rates.
items.tweetA: Gold above $4,200 with the 10-year near 5.4% and a firm dollar. That is not how gold is supposed to trade. Somebody is buying it as something other than a real-rate instrument. $GLD $GDX
items.tweetB: Equities at records and gold at $4,200 on the same morning. Either one of them is wrong or the hedge ratio has quietly gone up for everyone. I suspect the latter.

items.title: LatAm CAPE is cheap: US trades on ~3x the PE10 of the LatAm average
items.idea: EWZ jumped +20% in two weeks and ILF is up 25%+ YTD. On PE10 (price vs 10-year average earnings), average LatAm (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru) is cheap vs its own history, cheap vs EM, and the US trades at about 3x its PE10. ILF is ~40% financials and ~35% energy/materials, which Thomas calls a feature while commodities are in an updraft.
items.angle: Commodity-heavy value vs mega-cap growth rotation. 3x PE10 gap plus oil above $100 and gold above $4,200 is a cross-asset story.
items.tweetA: US CAPE is about 3x LatAm's. LatAm is 35% energy and materials in a world with Brent at $103 and gold at $4,200. The valuation gap is the market's bet that commodities mean-revert. I'm not sure they do. $ILF $EWZ
items.tweetB: EWZ is +20% in two weeks and people are asking if they missed it. On CAPE the answer is that the rerating hasn't started. The risk is not valuation, it's that the US 10-year at 5.4% drains EM flows.

charts.desc: PE10/CAPE by region: LatAm avg vs EM vs US (US ~3x). 🔥 Bonus: LatAm index at former early-2010s support, now overhead resistance.

items.title: LatAm index sits under old support turned resistance — wants a clean breakout plus commodities through ATH
items.idea: Bonus chart: the early-2010s support line is now a 'powerful zone of overhead resistance'. Thomas wants a clean breakout, commodities pushing beyond all-time highs, and global growth to pass 'a couple of impending tests' before gaining conviction.
items.angle: Technical gate for the value thesis; breakout needs commodities confirmation.
items.tweetA: Cheap is not a catalyst. LatAm needs to clear a decade-old resistance line AND commodities need new highs. Two conditions, not one. Until then it's a value trap with good PR. $ILF
items.tweetB: The LatAm trade is a levered bet on commodities making new highs. If you want that, there are cleaner ways to own it than a 40% bank ETF.

items.title: Meta's Muse agent costs $3 to $130 per user per month to serve
items.idea: Morgan Stanley (Nowak) puts a $775 base target on Meta, Top Pick. The note estimates Muse costs anywhere from roughly $3 to $130 per user per month to serve depending on usage, and meaningful agent monetization may not arrive until late 2027 or 2028. Slower user growth lowers the compute bill but pushes the transaction marketplace out too.
items.angle: A 40x spread in unit cost is a usage-mix problem, not a scale problem. Cost-per-token deflation versus heavier agent workloads.
items.tweetA: $3 to $130 per user per month. That's a 43x range on the same product, depending on how hard people use it. At 3 billion users, the low end is $100B a year. The high end is a different company. $META
items.tweetB: The question for every consumer agent isn't 'will they use it' but 'who are the power users and what do they pay'. Muse's heaviest users cost 43x the lightest. Free tier math gets ugly fast. $META $GOOGL

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Morgan Stanley (Brian Nowak)
items.title: Meta rerated from ~14x to ~21x forward earnings before Muse monetizes
items.idea: Meta has moved from roughly 14x to around 21x forward earnings. Morgan Stanley's argument: Meta has the compute, distribution and balance sheet; its moat is willingness to spend before economics are obvious. The author's caveat: at 21x 'execution matters'; agent monetization is late 2027/2028.
items.angle: 7 turns of multiple expansion paid for in advance. Capex-first moats get paid when ROIC shows up.
items.tweetA: Meta added 7 turns of forward multiple before Muse earns a dollar. The market is paying 2028 prices in 2026. That's fine if you believe the 2028 numbers. Just know that's the trade. $META
items.tweetB: Spend-before-economics is a moat until the 10-year makes duration expensive. Meta at 21x in a 5.4% world is long-duration equity. Not the same as the 14x Meta.

items.title: Record-high Brent short positioning meets the lowest visible onshore crude inventory ever
items.idea: First time in history of lowest visible global onshore crude inventory alongside the highest relative Brent short positioning. In July short positioning was a hair from record and implied a 4-5M b/d surplus that never materialized; inventories have trended lower since. Brent net long is also ~1/3 of 2018 and 2022 levels despite less inventory and more supply risk.
items.angle: Positioning vs fundamentals divergence. Crowded short into the tightest stocks on record is a squeeze set-up.
items.tweetA: Highest relative Brent short positioning ever. Lowest onshore crude inventory ever. Both at once. One of those datasets is wrong, and it isn't the one counting barrels. $BNO $USO
items.tweetB: In 2018 and 2022 there were three times the net longs and more inventory cushion. The market is more bearish now with less barrels in tanks. That is the part I can't make add up either.

charts.desc: Brent short position vs global onshore crude inventory; net long vs inventory; Brent price vs inventory. 🔥 First chart (record short vs record-low stocks).

items.title: Backwardation killed the bears: BNO at all-time high while Brent 'only' sits near $100
items.idea: Brent holding ~$100 looks like the bears are right, but backwardation wiped them out: BNO (rolls Brent monthly, collecting backwardation) is at an ATH. The author notes the short is Brent-only: cash-settled Brent shows huge shorts, physically settled WTI and other physical oil don't — which hints at a pair trade versus cracks, or something odd. He expects inventories to fall further post 'Peak Hormuz'.
items.angle: Roll yield as the real P&L driver; flat-price chart hides it. Cash-settled vs physical divergence.
items.tweetA: Brent is flat around $100. BNO is at an all-time high. The difference is roll yield. Anyone shorting flat price in a backwardated curve is paying for the privilege. Check the curve, not the chart. $BNO
items.tweetB: Shorts concentrated in cash-settled Brent, not in physical WTI. When the people who would have to deliver aren't the ones short, I'd ask who the shorts actually are. $USO $VLO

items.title: Army's 10-day AI test at Fort Irwin: 110F heat, servers overheated, batteries died
items.idea: WSJ: 9,700 soldiers, ten days in July in the Mojave vs a PLA-playing unit. Temperatures neared 110F, servers overheated, batteries couldn't be recharged, soldiers draped ice-water-soaked T-shirts over antennas. An Anduril drone was forced down by heat; a swarm of five small drones turned back when three Black Hawks entered its airspace. Drones flew at half max flight time with no AI help; AR headsets showed deficiencies despite three $100M+ contracts.
items.angle: Gap between pitch deck and desert. Power, thermal and batteries again the constraints, same as data centers.
items.tweetA: The US Army's AI test: servers overheated, batteries wouldn't charge, soldiers cooled antennas with wet T-shirts. Thermals and power are the bottleneck of AI everywhere, from Fort Irwin to Abilene. $ETN $VRT
items.tweetB: Three $100M+ contracts for AR headsets that 'showed deficiencies'. The defense AI trade is priced like the product ships next quarter. The Mojave says it doesn't.

items.title: Ukraine: 0.8M drones (2023) to 7M target (2026); US builds ~100k combat drones a year
items.idea: Ukraine made about 800,000 drones in 2023, 2.2M in 2024, 4M+ in 2025, targets 7M in 2026. The US makes ~100,000 combat drones a year (Bloomberg). Ukrainian operators took out a US armored brigade in German drills. One hidden Ukrainian plant makes ~1,000 drones/day at ~$500 each; a Kyiv researcher says drones cause ~80% of Russia's losses since early 2024. Magura sea drones sank three Russian warships; 100+ drones hit bombers in Siberia in June 2025.
items.angle: Manufacturing throughput is the strategic variable; 70x gap vs the US at scale.
items.tweetA: Ukraine: 7 million drones this year. US: about 100,000. A 70x gap, and the country with the smaller number has the bigger defense budget. Industrial capacity, not dollars, decides the next war. $AVAV $KTOS
items.tweetB: One Ukrainian plant: 1,000 drones a day at $500. Last year's Pentagon drone programs target $2,300 a unit. A 4.6x cost gap before you count the fielding speed. That's the number procurement has to close.

items.title: Defense tech VC: record $19.8B in Q1 across 262 deals; early-stage at 17-50x revenue
items.idea: PitchBook: $19.8B into defense tech Q1 2026, up from ~$5.7B in Q1 2024; including space, quantum, chips and nuclear H1 was $35.6B. Anduril raised $5B at $61B (doubled in about a year); Shield AI $12.7B; Saronic $9.25B. Fortune: early-stage defense startups fetch 17-50x revenue; Anduril's CEO admits 'a bit of a bubble' and its cofounder warns of down rounds. Shield AI still isn't a program of record.
items.angle: Valley-of-death between pilot and program of record is where the bubble pops. 3.5x VC run-rate in two years.
items.tweetA: Defense VC went from $5.7B to $19.8B a quarter in two years. Valuations of 17-50x revenue assume the Pentagon buys at Ukraine speed. Fort Irwin says the Pentagon buys at Pentagon speed. Down rounds are coming. $PLTR $AVAV
items.tweetB: Anduril doubled to $61B in about a year, and the CEO himself says 'a bit of a bubble'. When insiders call the froth, the late money is the exit liquidity.

items.title: $1.5T FY27 defense request (+42%); autonomous warfare group asks $53.6B vs $226M this year
items.idea: White House asks $1.5T for FY27, up 42% ($1.15T base + $350B reconciliation); House and Senate bills sit at $1.15T. The new Defense Autonomous Warfare Group asks $53.6B for all unmanned efforts vs $226M — but that mostly consolidates existing spend. Drone Dominance targets ~340,000 small attack drones by early 2028 with unit cost falling from $5,000 to ~$2,300; the Army wants 1M drones in 2-3 years. F-47 still gets ~$5B and shipbuilding $65.8B.
items.angle: Headline vs real marginal dollar: both chambers are ~$350B below request; the reconciliation piece is the swing.
items.tweetA: $226M to $53.6B for autonomous warfare looks like a 237x jump. Most of it is accounting: existing unmanned budgets moved under one roof. The real number to watch is the $350B reconciliation gap between the request and both chambers. $LMT $RTX
items.tweetB: Pentagon wants 340,000 drones at $2,300 each. That's $780M — about 12 F-35s. Price discovery is moving from $92M jets to $2,300 airframes. The primes' margin structure was built for the first number.

items.title: One Ford-class carrier = ~380,000 Shahed-class drones; Iranian drones even hit AWS data centers in the UAE
items.idea: Cost compression: Ford-class carrier $13.3B, F-35A ~$92M, Patriot interceptor ~$4M, Tomahawk ~$1.3M vs ~$35,000 for a LUCAS drone (US copy of the Shahed). The math cuts both ways: Iranian drones costing tens of thousands met with million-dollar interceptors. Shahed drones struck AWS data centers in the UAE in March and disrupted another in Bahrain.
items.angle: Cost-exchange ratio as the new strategic metric; Gulf data-center risk is a live AI-infra variable.
items.tweetA: A $4M Patriot to stop a $35K drone is a 114:1 cost exchange against the defender. And those drones already hit AWS data centers in the UAE. Gulf AI-campus buildouts are priced for zero of this. $AMZN $MSFT
items.tweetB: A carrier costs the same as 380,000 Shaheds. The Navy is organized around 11 of them. China built hundreds of anti-ship missiles for exactly that. $HII $GD

items.title: US vs China in drone war: software edge vs factory edge; DJI ~70% of world drones, shipbuilding 232x
items.idea: US leads in frontier models, leading-edge chips and the venture machine; China leads in manufacturing for drones, batteries and robots. DJI ~70% of commercial drones; China can reportedly build millions a year (Morgan Stanley). China's 2026 defense budget is 1.91T yuan (~$277B, +7%); PLA tested the Jiu Tian drone mothership (100-150 drones). A US Navy slide put Chinese shipbuilding capacity at ~232x the US. The FCC's December foreign-drone ban plus up to 100% tariffs leave US buyers with few options; China's robot dogs trace to US DoD-funded research.
items.angle: Tariffs plus bans create a captive US market with no domestic supply yet; the domestic ecosystem needs years.
items.tweetA: DJI makes 70% of the world's drones. The US banned them in December and tariffed the rest up to 100%. Congratulations: a protected market with no producers. Whoever builds the domestic supply chain gets the monopoly. $RCAT $UMAC
items.tweetB: US invents, China manufactures. Robot dogs and drone swarms both started in US-funded labs. The 232x shipbuilding gap is the number that should worry people more than any chip export rule.

items.title: Defense budgets are jobs budgets: TX, CA, VA each get ~$50B+/yr; Virginia $8,646 per resident
items.idea: States Newsroom: Texas, California and Virginia each got ~$50B+ per year since FY2020. Virginia received ~$8,646 per resident in FY24; Tarrant County TX over $120B in five years. Carriers and fighters survive because they spread jobs over many districts; a $2,300 drone has no constituency yet. Anduril's Arsenal-1 in Ohio (4,000 jobs) is how new weapons find votes.
items.angle: Political economy sets the calendar: old and new funded side by side for years.
items.tweetA: Virginia gets $8,646 per resident in defense spending. That's why carriers outlive their usefulness: every district has a piece. A $2,300 drone needs its own Arsenal-1 before it gets a vote. $GD $HII
items.tweetB: The cost curve decides who wins eventually, Congress decides when. Anduril building 4,000 jobs in Ohio is lobbying disguised as a factory.

items.title: Smaller states leapfrog: South Korea to train 500,000 'drone warriors'; Nvidia Jetsons found in Russian autonomous drones
items.idea: Turkey's Baykar TB2 signed by 34 countries; South Korea (June) to train 500,000 drone operators and field 110,000 drones by 2029; Ukraine turned a battlefield feedback loop into an industry. Darker side: Ukrainian examiners found consumer Nvidia Jetson modules, marked Made in China and bought on resale markets, in wreckage of fully autonomous Russian drones.
items.angle: General-purpose AI chips are an uncontrollable input; export-control leakage visible in the wreckage.
items.tweetA: Ukrainian forensics found Nvidia Jetsons in autonomous Russian drones, bought on resale markets. Export controls on datacenter GPUs don't touch a $300 edge module. The real chip war is at the low end. $NVDA
items.tweetB: South Korea will train 500,000 drone operators. That's a conscription-scale bet that drones are standard issue. Watch Seoul's procurement, not just Washington's. $005930.KS

items.title: Bond illusion: duration doesn't protect when markets fall; a 3% coupon at 4% inflation is real impoverishment
items.idea: The author argues bonds aren't a shield: when rates rise, prices fall and duration amplifies it; savers who thought long bonds were safe have taken large drawdowns. Bonds hedge neither inflation (3% yield vs 4% inflation = real loss) nor FX. Proper role: high-quality, 1-3 year (short) or 3-5 year (mid) cash-parking. Beyond that it's speculation on the curve. For coupon income, stop watching daily prices.
items.angle: Retail narrative reset after the 5.4% 10-year. Note the pitch itself is a sentiment gauge.
items.tweetA: Italian retail is being told bonds don't protect when stocks crash, 10y at 5.4%. That's the 2022 lesson arriving four years late, and usually the lesson arrives right before the move reverses. $TLT $BTP
items.tweetB: 3% coupon in 4% inflation is a real loss no matter who issues it. That line is aimed at savers; the same math applies to every pension duration book.

items.title: OpenAI reportedly missed revenue expectations by ~$20B (expected ~$70B, landed ~$50B)
items.idea: Newsletter intro: tech comments this week included OpenAI missing expected revenue by ~$20B (expected near $70B, ended near $50B). The author compares AI to the early-2020s self-driving hiccup (Tesla/Waymo/Mobileye): when growth hits a valley, firms either hide behind moral arguments or reset goals. (Remainder of the post truncated/paywalled in email.)
items.angle: A 29% revenue miss at the lead lab against $1T committed capex. Watch for guidance reset vs capex.
items.tweetA: OpenAI: expected ~$70B, got ~$50B. A 29% miss. The compute commitments were sized to the first number. Someone is going to be holding capacity sized for revenue that isn't there. $NVDA $ORCL $MSFT
items.tweetB: Self-driving went from 'five years away' to a decade of grinding. If AI revenue misses 29% at the leader, the buildout phase and the monetization phase are further apart than the capex curve assumes.

items.title: Microsoft pushing for an 'emergency brake' on advanced AI
items.idea: Alongside the OpenAI miss, the author says Microsoft is pushing for an 'emergency brake' on advanced AI, and frames it as the typical response when growth hits a valley: hide behind moral arguments ('AI might kill us all') or rearrange the goals. Title also teases a yield-curve angle ('Yield Curve Makes it Worse'), not visible in the preview.
items.angle: Safety framing as incumbent moat/slowdown cover; regulatory capture reading.
items.tweetA: Microsoft wants an 'emergency brake' on advanced AI in the same week OpenAI misses revenue by $20B. A brake is also a way to explain slower growth. Watch who asks for rules when the S-curve flattens. $MSFT
items.tweetB: Every industry asks for regulation when the easy growth ends. Incumbents with the capex already sunk benefit most from a brake on everyone else.
